title: YOU WANTED HEALING TO MEAN YOU NEVER HURT AGAIN. SOMETIMES HEALING MEANS THE WOUND NO LONGER GETS TO RULE YOU.
paragraphs: YOU WANTED HEALING TO MEAN YOU NEVER HURT AGAIN. SOMETIMES HEALING MEANS THE WOUND NO LONGER GETS TO RULE YOU.
Maybe the proof that Jesus is healing you isn't that you can no longer remember what happened. Maybe it's that what happened can no longer decide who you become.
You prayed for healing.
But if you're honest, you had a particular definition of healing in mind.
You thought healing meant forgetting.
You thought one morning you would wake up and their name wouldn't tighten something inside your chest anymore.
You thought the anniversary would eventually become just another square on the calendar.
You thought the betrayal would stop replaying in your mind.
You thought you would walk into that familiar place and feel absolutely nothing.
No shaking hands.
No memories.
No questions.
No tears.
You thought healing meant becoming the person you were before it happened.
And because you're still hurting sometimes, a frightening thought has begun whispering in the quiet:
Maybe God hasn't healed me.
Maybe you've even wondered whether something is wrong with your faith.
Because Christians sometimes know how to celebrate dramatic testimonies better than slow ones.
We understand, “I was broken, Jesus touched me, and everything changed.”
And praise God when that happens.
But what about the testimony that sounds like this?
“I still remember.”
“I still have difficult days.”
“I still cry sometimes.”
“But I don't live there anymore.”
What if that is also a testimony?
What if you have misunderstood what healing can look like?
Because Scripture gives us an image of God that is far more tender than the demand to “just get over it.”
Psalm 147:3 says:
“He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.”
The Hebrew is painfully beautiful:
הָרֹפֵא לִשְׁבוּרֵי לֵב וּמְחַבֵּשׁ לְעַצְּבוֹתָם
Hā-rōfē’ lishvurei lev, u-meḥabbēsh le‘atzevotam.
“He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.”
Don't rush past that picture.
God does not mock the wounded.
He does not stand across the room shouting, “Why aren't you over this yet?”
He comes near.
He heals.
He binds.
The Hebrew verb translated “heals” comes from רָפָא — rāfā’, meaning to heal, cure, or restore.
But then Scripture gives us another word.
וּמְחַבֵּשׁ — u-meḥabbēsh.
“And He binds up.”
It comes from חָבַשׁ — ḥābash, a word associated with binding or wrapping.
Do you see the tenderness in that?
A wound that is being bound is still a wound.
It hasn't been denied.
It hasn't been called imaginary.
It hasn't been erased from history.
It is being cared for.
Maybe someone needs to hear that tonight.
Being wounded and being abandoned are not the same thing.
And still feeling pain does not automatically mean God has stopped working.
Sometimes the deepest evidence of healing isn't that the wound disappeared.
It's that the wound lost its throne.
There was a time when what happened controlled everything.
It controlled how you trusted.
How you loved.
How you slept.
How you saw yourself.
How you interpreted silence.
How quickly you panicked when somebody's tone changed.
How terrified you became when someone you loved seemed distant.
Maybe someone betrayed you so deeply that now innocent people occasionally pay emotional debts they never created.
Maybe somebody walked away.
Maybe somebody died.
Maybe your marriage collapsed.
Maybe a parent failed you.
Maybe someone you trusted in church wounded you.
Maybe somebody made promises before God and later behaved as though those promises had never existed.
Maybe what happened wasn't one dramatic event.
Maybe it was years.
Years of being ignored.
Years of manipulation.
Years of rejection.
Years of pretending everything was fine because explaining what was happening felt impossible.
And then you finally escaped the situation...
but discovered the situation had not completely escaped you.
That's the part nobody warned you about.
You can leave the room and still carry the room inside you.
You can delete the messages and still remember the words.
You can forgive someone and still grieve what their choices cost you.
You can genuinely love Jesus and still need time to learn how to trust again.
You can know Romans 8:28 and still cry.
You can believe in resurrection while standing beside a grave.
Even Jesus did.
John 11 records one of Scripture's shortest and most devastating sentences:
“Jesus wept.”
He knew Lazarus was about to rise.
Think about that.
Jesus knew resurrection was coming...
and still wept.
So tears are not necessarily evidence that faith has failed.
Grief and hope can occupy the same heart.
Pain and faith can exist in the same prayer.
A person can be healing while still having tender places.
The Christian hope is not emotional numbness.
Our hope is Jesus Christ.
And Jesus does something far greater than teaching wounded people how to pretend nothing happened.
He redeems.
He restores.
He transforms.
He takes what sin intended to destroy and refuses to allow it to have the final word.
That doesn't mean every relationship will be restored.
Some relationships should not return to what they were.
Forgiveness does not automatically require renewed access.
Reconciliation requires more than one person's willingness; trust can require repentance, truth, wisdom, changed behavior, and time.
You can forgive someone before God while still establishing wise boundaries.
You can release vengeance without volunteering for another betrayal.
Jesus told His disciples to be “wise as serpents and innocent as doves.”
Grace is not stupidity.
Forgiveness is not pretending evil wasn't evil.
The cross itself proves that God takes sin too seriously to pretend it doesn't matter.
Our sin was so serious that redemption required the blood of Christ.
And God's grace is so astonishing that Christ willingly came to save sinners.
This is where healing becomes Gospel.
Because beneath every wound another problem eventually appears.
Our greatest problem is not merely what others have done to us.
It is also what sin has done within us.
Pain can become bitterness.
Betrayal can become hatred.
Fear can become control.
Grief can become despair.
Being sinned against can tempt us toward sin of our own.
And suddenly we discover that we need more than emotional recovery.
We need a Savior.
Jesus did not come merely to make wounded people feel better.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
He carried our sin to the cross.
He endured shame.
He shed His blood.
He died.
And on the third day, He rose.
The Gospel doesn't tell you your wound doesn't matter.
The Gospel tells you your wound does not get the final word because Jesus Christ does.
Maybe you have spent years asking Jesus to erase something He intends to redeem.
You keep praying:
“Lord, make me forget.”
And perhaps the deeper prayer eventually becomes:
“Lord, even if I remember, don't let this memory own me.”
That is a different prayer.
“Jesus, I still remember what they did...
but I refuse to become what they did.”
“I still remember being abandoned...
but abandonment will not become my identity.”
“I still remember being betrayed...
but betrayal will not teach me to hate.”
“I still remember the funeral...
but death will not convince me resurrection isn't coming.”
“I still have scars...
but my scars don't get to name me.”
Christ does.
That is healing without erasure.
And perhaps that's why scars are such a powerful Christian image.
After His resurrection, Jesus was unmistakably victorious, yet the Gospel of John records Him showing His disciples His hands and His side.
Victory did not require pretending crucifixion never happened.
The resurrection did not make Calvary unreal.
Calvary had happened.
The wounds had been real.
But death had lost authority over Him.
And there is something breathtaking in that.
Your story does not need to become unhappened for Jesus to redeem it.
God does not need to rewrite yesterday's historical facts in order to rewrite tomorrow.
He can take the chapter you would never have chosen and refuse to let that chapter become the ending.
That is what grace does.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Grace enters darkness carrying resurrection.
Maybe you're reading this while carrying a wound nobody around you knows exists.
You smile.
You work.
You worship.
You answer messages.
You tell everybody, “I'm okay.”
Then nighttime comes.
And something hurts again.
Please hear this carefully:
Don't measure God's faithfulness exclusively by how little pain you feel today.
Look also at what the pain can no longer make you do.
Maybe you still cry, but you don't run back to what destroyed you.
That's growth.
Maybe you still remember, but you don't fantasize about revenge anymore.
That's growth.
Maybe certain days still hurt, but you no longer believe your life ended there.
That's growth.
Maybe you still struggle to trust, but you're learning to place your deepest trust in Christ instead of another human being.
That's growth.
Maybe the wound occasionally speaks...
but it isn't preaching your identity anymore.
Jesus is.
And perhaps you haven't noticed how far God has already carried you because you have been measuring healing only by what remains instead of noticing what has changed.
Look again.
There was once a night you didn't think you would survive.
You survived it.
There was once a morning you couldn't imagine getting out of bed.
You got up.
There was once a betrayal you thought would destroy your ability to love forever.
Yet something inside you still wants goodness.
Still wants truth.
Still wants Jesus.
You are reading an article about healing because somewhere underneath the scar, hope is still breathing.
Don't worship your progress.
Don't make an idol out of becoming “strong.”
Look toward Christ.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of wounded people becoming impressive.
It is the story of helpless sinners being rescued by an astonishing Savior.
And maybe the next step in your healing isn't demanding that you never hurt again.
Maybe it is surrendering the hurt again.
“Jesus, this still hurts.”
That's a prayer.
“Jesus, I'm angry again.”
That's a prayer.
“Jesus, I thought I had forgiven them, but something came back today.”
Bring that too.
Repent wherever pain has produced sin in you.
Forgive as Christ commands you to forgive.
Seek wise, godly help where you need it.
Tell the truth.
Stop pretending.
Receive grace.
Keep walking.
Healing is not always a straight line.
And Scripture never tells us that every sorrow disappears in this present age.
In fact, Revelation points us toward a coming day when God Himself “will wipe away every tear,” and death, mourning, crying, and pain will finally be gone.
That means Christianity offers something much stronger than the promise of an easier week.
It offers resurrection.
A new creation.
Christ forever.
A world in which the last tear really will be the last tear.
Until then, we walk with scars.
We worship through tears.
We forgive while remembering what forgiveness cost.
We learn boundaries.
We repent.
We fall.
We get up.
We keep coming back to Jesus.
And little by little, wounds that once commanded us become places where God's mercy becomes visible.
One day you may sit beside someone who has just experienced what nearly destroyed you.
They will look at you with swollen eyes and say:
“I don't think I'm going to survive this.”
And suddenly you will understand something.
You won't give them a cliché.
You won't tell them to get over it.
You'll sit beside them.
Because you remember.
And perhaps you'll whisper:
“I know it doesn't feel possible right now. But stay close to Jesus. One day this pain may still be part of your story without being the ruler of your story.”
That's when scars become ministry.
Not because suffering was good.
But because God is so redemptive that He can bring good even from what was evil.
Joseph could eventually look back on devastating human betrayal and recognize God's sovereign hand bringing good from what others intended for evil.
The cross is the supreme demonstration.
Human beings committed history's greatest injustice against the sinless Son of God.
Yet through that very cross, God accomplished redemption for sinners.
From scandal...
to grace.
That is our story.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling betrayal beautiful.
Not by calling abuse good.
Not by telling mourners they shouldn't mourn.
But by declaring that sin, shame, betrayal, suffering, Satan, and death do not possess the authority to write the final sentence.
Jesus does.
So perhaps today you need to stop condemning yourself because healing has taken longer than you expected.
Bring the wound back to Christ.
Again.
And tomorrow, if necessary...
again.
The same God who “heals the brokenhearted” is also the God who “binds up their wounds.”
Bandaging implies tenderness.
Attention.
Care.
And sometimes process.
God knows exactly where it hurts.
Psalm 147 moves almost immediately from God binding broken hearts to God numbering the stars and calling them by name.
The One whose attention reaches the heavens is not too occupied for your broken heart.
You have not disappeared from His sight.
And if you're reading this with tears in your eyes, don't rush away from this moment.
Talk to Jesus.
Not polished Christian language.
Truth.
Tell Him what still hurts.
Tell Him what you're angry about.
Confess where bitterness has taken root.
Confess where you have sinned because you were sinned against.
Ask Him for grace to forgive.
Ask for wisdom about boundaries.
Ask Him to restore what should be restored and give you courage to release what should not.
And above everything else, ask Him to make you more like Christ.
Because the greatest healing isn't merely becoming comfortable again.
It is belonging to Jesus and being transformed by Him.
And if you have spent months or years pretending you're completely fine, maybe today your confession is only three words:
“No more hiding.”
Someone reading those words may realize they aren't alone.
And if you know someone who has been discouraged because their healing is taking longer than they expected, send this article to them.
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns favor with God. It doesn't.

If this ministry helps keep you close to Scripture, stay connected. Invite your family. Invite the friend struggling with faith. Invite the believer who has grown cold. Invite the person who isn't even sure they believe yet.
Come to Jesus.
Not the stronger version of you.
Not the healed-enough version.
Not the version who finally stopped crying.
You.
Right now.
With the wound.
With the questions.
With the memory.
With the parts of your heart that still flinch.
Come to Christ.
Because perhaps healing was never supposed to mean that you could look backward and feel absolutely nothing.
Perhaps sometimes healing looks like looking backward and realizing:
“That happened to me...
but it does not own me.
It wounded me...
but it does not name me.
I remember it...
but I no longer worship at its grave.
Jesus found me there.
Jesus carried me from there.
Jesus is still healing me.
And Jesus—not my wound—gets the final word.”
And remember this when the scar aches again:
The wound may remain part of your testimony, but because of Jesus, it no longer has to remain the author of your identity.
